Introduction"},{"page":5,"text":"HTTP semantics ([HTTP]) are used for a broad range ofservices on the Internet. These semantics"},{"page":5,"text":"have most commonly been used with HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2. HTTP/1.1 has been used over a variety"},{"page":5,"text":"oftransport and session layers, while HTTP/2 has been used primarily with TLS over TCP. HTTP/3"},{"page":5,"text":"supports the same semantics over a new transport protocol: QUIC."},{"page":5,"text":"1.1. Prior Versions of HTTP"},{"page":5,"text":"HTTP/1.1 ([HTTP/1.1]) uses whitespace-delimited text ﬁelds to convey HTTP messages. While these"},{"page":5,"text":"exchanges are human readable, using whitespace for message formatting leads to parsing"},{"page":5,"text":"complexity and excessive tolerance ofvariant behavior."},{"page":5,"text":"Because HTTP/1.1 does not include a multiplexing layer, multiple TCP connections are often used"},{"page":5,"text":"to service requests in parallel. However, that has a negative impact on congestion control and"},{"page":5,"text":"network eﬃciency, since TCP does not share congestion control across multiple connections."},{"page":5,"text":"HTTP/2 ([HTTP/2]) introduced a binary framing and multiplexing layer to improve latency"},{"page":5,"text":"without modifying the transport layer. However, because the parallel nature ofHTTP/2's"},{"page":5,"text":"multiplexing is not visible to TCP's loss recovery mechanisms, a lost or reordered packet causes"},{"page":5,"text":"all active transactions to experience a stall regardless ofwhether that transaction was directly"},{"page":5,"text":"impacted by the lost packet."},{"page":5,"text":"1.2. Delegation to QUIC"},{"page":5,"text":"The QUIC transport protocol incorporates stream multiplexing and per-stream ﬂow control,"},{"page":5,"text":"similar to that provided by the HTTP/2 framing layer. By providing reliability at the stream level"},{"page":5,"text":"and congestion control across the entire connection, QUIC has the capability to improve the"},{"page":5,"text":"performance ofHTTP compared to a TCP mapping. QUIC also incorporates TLS 1.3 ([TLS]) at the"},{"page":5,"text":"transport layer, oﬀering comparable conﬁdentiality and integrity to running TLS over TCP, with"},{"page":5,"text":"the improved connection setup latency ofTCP Fast Open ([TFO])."},{"page":5,"text":"This document deﬁnes HTTP/3: a mapping ofHTTP semantics over the QUIC transport protocol,"},{"page":5,"text":"drawing heavily on the design ofHTTP/2. HTTP/3 relies on QUIC to provide conﬁdentiality and"},{"page":5,"text":"integrity protection of data; peer authentication; and reliable, in-order, per-stream delivery."},{"page":5,"text":"While delegating stream lifetime and ﬂow-control issues to QUIC, a binary framing similar to the"},{"page":5,"text":"HTTP/2 framing is used on each stream. Some HTTP/2 features are subsumed by QUIC, while other"},{"page":5,"text":"features are implemented atop QUIC."},{"page":5,"text":"QUIC is described in [QUIC-TRANSPORT]. For a full description ofHTTP/2, see [HTTP/2]."},{"page":5,"text":"Bishop Standards Track Page 5"},{"page":6,"text":"RFC 9114 HTTP/3 June 2022"},{"page":6,"text":"2. HTTP/3 Protocol Overview"},{"page":6,"text":"HTTP/3 provides a transport for HTTP semantics using the QUIC transport protocol and an"},{"page":6,"text":"internal framing layer similar to HTTP/2."},{"page":6,"text":"Once a client knows that an HTTP/3 server exists at a certain endpoint, it opens a QUIC"},{"page":6,"text":"connection. QUIC provides protocol negotiation, stream-based multiplexing, and ﬂow control."},{"page":6,"text":"Discovery of an HTTP/3 endpoint is described in Section 3.1."},{"page":6,"text":"Within each stream, the basic unit ofHTTP/3 communication is a frame (Section 7.2). Each frame"},{"page":6,"text":"type serves a diﬀerent purpose. For example, HEADERS and DATA frames form the basis ofHTTP"},{"page":6,"text":"requests and responses (Section 4.1). Frames that apply to the entire connection are conveyed on"},{"page":6,"text":"a dedicated control stream."},{"page":6,"text":"Multiplexing ofrequests is performed using the QUIC stream abstraction, which is described in"},{"page":6,"text":"Section 2 of [QUIC-TRANSPORT]. Each request-response pair consumes a single QUIC stream."},{"page":6,"text":"Streams are independent of each other, so one stream that is blocked or suﬀers packet loss does"},{"page":6,"text":"not prevent progress on other streams."},{"page":6,"text":"Server push is an interaction mode introduced in HTTP/2 ([HTTP/2]) that permits a server to push"},{"page":6,"text":"a request-response exchange to a client in anticipation ofthe client making the indicated request."},{"page":6,"text":"This trades oﬀnetwork usage against a potential latency gain. Several HTTP/3 frames are used to"},{"page":6,"text":"manage server push, such as PUSH_PROMISE, MAX_PUSH_ID, and CANCEL_PUSH."},{"page":6,"text":"As in HTTP/2, request and response ﬁelds are compressed for transmission. Because HPACK"},{"page":6,"text":"([HPACK]) relies on in-order transmission of compressed ﬁeld sections (a guarantee not provided"},{"page":6,"text":"by QUIC), HTTP/3 replaces HPACKwith QPACK ([QPACK]). QPACK uses separate unidirectional"},{"page":6,"text":"streams to modify and track ﬁeld table state, while encoded ﬁeld sections refer to the state ofthe"},{"page":6,"text":"table without modifying it."},{"page":6,"text":"2.1. Document Organization"},{"page":6,"text":"The following sections provide a detailed overview ofthe lifecycle of an HTTP/3 connection:"},{"page":6,"text":"• \"Connection Setup and Management\" (Section 3) covers how an HTTP/3 endpoint is"},{"page":6,"text":"discovered and an HTTP/3 connection is established."},{"page":6,"text":"• \"Expressing HTTP Semantics in HTTP/3\" (Section 4) describes how HTTP semantics are"},{"page":6,"text":"expressed using frames."},{"page":6,"text":"• \"Connection Closure\" (Section 5) describes how HTTP/3 connections are terminated, either"},{"page":6,"text":"gracefully or abruptly."},{"page":6,"text":"The details ofthe wire protocol and interactions with the transport are described in subsequent"},{"page":6,"text":"sections:"},{"page":6,"text":"• \"Stream Mapping and Usage\" (Section 6) describes the way QUIC streams are used."},{"page":6,"text":"• \"HTTP Framing Layer\" (Section 7) describes the frames used on most streams."},{"page":6,"text":"Bishop Standards Track Page 6"},{"page":7,"text":"RFC 9114 HTTP/3 June 2022"},{"page":7,"text":"• \"Error Handling\" (Section 8) describes how error conditions are handled and expressed,"},{"page":7,"text":"either on a particular stream or for the connection as a whole."},{"page":7,"text":"Additional resources are provided in the ﬁnal sections:"}]}
